Inflammation plays an important role in Cardiovascular disease (CVD) pathogenesis as the main cause of mortality in hemodialysis (HD) patients. Despite the relevance of nutrition and dietary intakes for inflammation status, the role of dietary protein sources remains unclear. The aim of this study was to evaluate the association between the different types of dietary protein and pentraxin 3 (PTX3) levels in HD patients. In this multi-center cross-sectional study, 227 adult patients undergoing HD for a minimum 90 days were recruited. A validated 168-item food frequency questionnaire was used to assess dietary intakes. Also, 5 ml blood samples were collected from each patient to measure the concentration of serum PTX3. Overall, 227 patients, including 63 women and 164 men, with a mean age of 58 years, participated in this study. There was a greater intake of animal protein per kilogram dry weight among patients with higher levels of PTX3 (0.46 vs. 0.54 g/kg; P = 0.035). In contrast, consumption of total protein and plant protein per kilogram dry weight was not different across PTX3 levels. Moreover, the chance of increased PTX3 concentration was directly associated with a one-unit increase in animal protein intake per kilogram dry weight, after adjusting for confounders. We did not observe any association between one-unit increases in plant protein intake per kilogram dry weight and chance of increased PTX3. In conclusion, animal protein intake was directly associated with circulating PTX3. Subject terms Nutrition End-stage renal disease issue-copyright-statement © Springer Nature Limited 2023 Introduction Hemodialysis (HD) is the main form of renal replacement therapy for most patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) 1 . Unfortunately, the mortality rate in HD patients is significantly higher than the general population 2 . Epidemiologic studies showed that cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) are the main cause of the mortality in HD patients 3 , whilst inflammation plays an important role in CVD pathogenesis among HD patients 4 , which can lead to adverse clinical outcomes 5 , 6 . Inflammatory markers are commonly used in early diagnosis, prognosis, and monitoring of renal disease and considered as a predictor of mortality 7 . Pentraxin 3 (PTX3) is a novel inflammatory biomarker that has been assessed in recent studies 8 . PTX3 as a member of the pentraxin superfamily, and responsible for modulating immune-inflammatory responses 9 . As opposed to nonspecific biomarkers of inflammation, including C-reactive protein (CRP) and serum amyloid P mainly produced by hepatic cells 10 , production of PTX3 occurs in cells which have a contribution to the onset and progression of CVD, such as vascular endothelial cells, fibroblasts, smooth muscle cells, epithelial cells, myeloid cells, and lymphatic cells 9 . Therefore, PTX3 is considered as a specific and sensitive indicator that can connect inflammation to CVD 11 . Moreover, PTX3 is related to renal functions 12 , 13 and considered as an independent predictor of mortality among CKD patients 14 . Previous study reported that Spearman's rank correlation coefficient between PTX3 and CRP was 0.157 (P = 0.013) in patients with ESRD 15 . Nutrition and dietary intakes are among the most important factors influencing the inflammation status in HD patients 16 . Malnutrition, as a cause of inflammation, is prevalent among these patients, resultant from decreasing amounts of dietary protein intake to slow down progression of chronic kidney disease (CKD) 17 . Nevertheless, the role of dietary protein sources in inflammation status has been neglected 18 . Results of a recent meta-analysis demonstrated a favorable relationship between a healthy dietary pattern (i.e., consuming more plant proteins and fish, along with less red meat) and mortality risk in CKD patients 19 . Moreover, a vegetarian diet can be recommended to adults with CKD because it can provide more protein with less bioavailable phosphorus 20 , and reduce uremic toxin levels 21 , hypertension 22 , metabolic acidosis 23 , and inflammation 24 . A systematic review and meta-analysis reported that in comparison with total protein intake, animal proteins elevated CRP concentration. Also, a decreasing trend in CRP was reported when plant proteins compared with animal proteins in adults with CKD 25 .Although previous studies have showed that animal protein had adverse effects on CRP concentration, the association between the sources of dietary protein and levels of PTX3 has not been assessed in HD patients. Therefore, we aimed to evaluate the association between different types of dietary protein (animal vs. plant) and levels of circulating PTX3.

core_effect_and_quantification.magnitude_quantification: Patients with higher PTX3 levels consumed more animal protein (0.54 g/kg vs 0.46 g/kg dry weight; P = 0.035). A one-unit increase in animal protein intake per kilogram dry weight was directly associated with increased PTX3 (OR = 3.123, 95% CI 1.077-9.053, P = 0.036 in Model 1; OR = 4.524, 95% CI 1.247-16.417, P = 0.022 in Model 2), leading to significantly increased circulating levels of PTX3.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Dietary protein intake (animal vs. plant) and its impact on inflammation and metabolic processes in hemodialysis (HD) and chronic kidney disease (CKD)/end-stage renal disease (ESRD) patients, including dialysis-related inflammation.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: Animal protein intake is directly associated with circulating PTX3 levels. PTX3 is a novel inflammatory biomarker that modulates immune-inflammatory responses. It is produced by cells contributing to CVD progression (vascular endothelial cells, fibroblasts, smooth muscle cells, epithelial cells, myeloid cells, and lymphatic cells), distinguishing it from non-specific biomarkers like CRP. PTX3 release occurs quickly from neutrophil granules in response to inflammatory signals. Animal protein intake negatively impacts the gut microbiome by producing ammonia and sulfur-based materials, leading to dysbiosis and inflammation. Cholesterol from animal fat/meat also contributes to inflammation, as circulating LDL cholesterol induces PTX3 expression. Furthermore, sulfur-containing amino acids in animal proteins enhance dietary acidity, exacerbating metabolic acidosis in CKD patients, which induces inflammation. In contrast, plant-based diets improve dysbiotic microflora by increasing short-chain fatty acids, inhibiting pathogens, reducing pro-inflammatory parameters, oxidative stress, and uremic toxins. Plant protein metabolization minimizes acid production and consequently reduces inflammatory markers.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: PTX3 is considered a specific and sensitive indicator that can connect inflammation to CVD, as its production occurs in cells contributing to CVD progression (e.g., vascular endothelial cells, fibroblasts, smooth muscle cells, epithelial cells, myeloid cells, lymphatic cells), as opposed to nonspecific biomarkers like CRP and serum amyloid P primarily produced by hepatic cells. PTX3 is also highlighted as a quick and sensitive indicator specifically of dialysis-related inflammation among HD patients, showing greater sensitivity to micro inflammatory processes than other inflammatory biomarkers in HD patients. While animal protein intake was specifically associated with increased PTX3 levels, its effects on other inflammatory biomarkers (e.g., chemerin, progranulin) are controversial.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Adult patients (aged 18 or older) undergoing hemodialysis (HD) for a minimum of 90 days, specifically those with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) and chronic kidney disease (CKD). Exclusions included enteral/parenteral nutrition, daily energy intake lower than 800 kcal/day or more than 4200 kcal/day, smokers, or recorded history of myocardial infarction. The study included patients from five HD centers in Isfahan, Iran.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: Increased animal protein intake is directly associated with higher levels of PTX3, a novel inflammatory biomarker. This elevated inflammation plays a significant role in cardiovascular disease (CVD) pathogenesis and is a predictor of mortality and adverse clinical outcomes in HD and CKD/ESRD patients. Permanent low-grade inflammation is a major concern in ESRD, exacerbating morbidity and mortality risk. The findings imply that dietary protein sources, particularly animal protein, can significantly influence inflammation status. Plant-based diets, in contrast, are associated with reduced inflammatory markers, improved kidney function, and mitigation of metabolic acidosis, offering protective benefits for chronic disease complications.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: Adverse risk: Animal protein intake is associated with increased inflammatory markers (PTX3, CRP), which predict higher mortality and cardiovascular disease risk in HD and CKD/ESRD patients, and can exacerbate metabolic acidosis and negatively impact kidney functions. Diagnostic utility: PTX3 serves as a quick, sensitive, and specific indicator for dialysis-related inflammation and overall inflammation linked to CVD progression.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: Pentraxin 3 (PTX3) is considered a novel, specific, and sensitive inflammatory biomarker that can connect inflammation to cardiovascular disease (CVD) and is an independent predictor of mortality among CKD patients. It is highlighted as a better predictor of inflammation than interleukin-6, tumor necrosis factor alpha, and C-reactive protein (CRP) due to its quick release from neutrophil granules in response to inflammatory signals and expression in a wide range of tissues. PTX3 demonstrates greater sensitivity to micro-inflammatory processes in HD patients than other inflammatory biomarkers. Serum PTX3 concentration was measured using ELISA kits (ZellBio GmbH, Germany) with acceptable Inter Assay CV (< 10%) and Intra Assay CV (< 12%). The 168-item semi-quantitative food frequency questionnaire (FFQ) used for dietary assessment has shown acceptable validity and reliability in the Iranian population.
recommended_alternatives: No specific alternative biomarkers are recommended directly, but further research is advised to identify the most reliable inflammatory biomarkers for predicting adverse outcomes in HD patients, as results for other biomarkers of inflammation can be controversial.
